ops.title: Prove a regression test fails without touching the tree: go test -overlay
ops.body:
Every falsifiability proof needs the same thing — run the suite against the UNFIXED code and watch the new test fail. The obvious methods are bad when other agents are editing the same working copy: mutating the file races them, and a worktree is heavyweight for a two-minute check.

`go test -overlay <json>` maps real paths to replacement files without writing to the tree:

```sh
jj file show -r @- internal/vcstest/shim.go > /tmp/pre/shim.go
cat > /tmp/overlay.json <<EOF
{"Replace": {"/abs/path/internal/vcstest/shim.go": "/tmp/pre/shim.go"}}
EOF
go test -overlay /tmp/overlay.json -race ./internal/vcstest/
```

That runs the suite against the committed version of exactly those files, with zero writes to the working copy. Used 2026-08-02 to reproduce a CI failure against pre-fix code while three lanes were concurrently editing the same package — the only method that worked without disturbing any of them.

Pairs well with `jj file show -r @-` (or any revision) to materialize the "before" side, and it composes: overlay several files at once to test a multi-file revert.

RELATED DISCIPLINE, same session: a regression test should keep a CONTROL assertion, not only the positive one. `TestScriptToolNeedsItsInterpreterOnPATH` (internal/vcstest) asserts that a script tool run under the bare system PATH exits **127** — the CI condition it was written for — before asserting the shim fixes it. If someone later simplifies the mechanism away, the positive half fails while the control keeps documenting why the mechanism existed at all. A test that only proves the fix works loses the record of what it was fixing.
